notes: Ruling slot 23 holds the Holy See itself under Paul VI and uses MD's Holy See sprite (HLS_western_autocracy); MD's slot 0 'Holy See' therefore gives way to the Pius XII-era curial anti-communist bloc ('Il Partito Romano'). The Curia's power centre (Secretariat of State with Villot, Benelli, Casaroli) is the non-aligned bureaucracy in 13. Lefebvre's traditionalists sit in 14 (Coetus network, then SSPX from 1970.11.1). Emerging slots hold Eastern-bloc Catholic collaborators (PAX, Opus Pacis); left slots hold Catholic dissent and liberation theology; Islamic slots hold Muslim bodies relevant to Vatican diplomacy (Lebanon, Iraq, Jerusalem, Saudi Arabia, Geneva).

0.name: Il Partito Romano
0.text:
The Roman Party is the name given to the curial bloc that dominated the Vatican under Pius XII: Italian prelates who saw the Church as the bulwark of the West against communism and pressed for alliances with the right in Italian politics. Its standard-bearers are Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, who retired from the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1968, and Cardinal Giuseppe Siri, Archbishop of Genoa and papabile in 1958 and 1963.

They distrust the Council's openness, Casaroli's dealings with communist governments and the softening of anti-communism under Paul VI. They want a Church allied firmly with Washington, NATO and Italy's anti-communist forces, governed from Rome with a firm hand. Their leverage lies in the older cardinals, the Roman congregations and friends among Italian conservatives and American Catholics.

1.name: Opus Dei
1.text:
Opus Dei was founded in Madrid in 1928 by the Spanish priest Josemaría Escrivá de Balaguer, who now directs it from its headquarters at Villa Tevere in Rome. Recognised as a secular institute, it counts tens of thousands of lay members and priests worldwide, and its members hold key ministries in the Spanish government formed in October 1969, where Laureano López Rodó directs the development plans.

The Work teaches the sanctification of ordinary professional life, combining doctrinal orthodoxy and loyalty to the Pope with modern management, universities and business schools. Politically it is conservative, firmly anti-communist and Western in outlook, and it seeks a juridical status independent of the bishops. Its leverage lies in its disciplined elite of professionals, bankers and ministers and its quiet influence in the Curia.

2.name: Societas Iesu
2.text:
The Society of Jesus, the largest religious order of men with some 30,000 members, has been led since 1965 by the Basque Superior General Pedro Arrupe, a missionary who survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima. The Jesuits run the Gregorian University, the review La Civiltà Cattolica and Vatican Radio, and their theologians, above all Karl Rahner, shaped the reforms of the Second Vatican Council.

Under Arrupe the order is turning toward dialogue with the modern world, ecumenism, the social sciences and justice for the poor, to the growing unease of conservatives in the Curia. It favours collegiality, freedom of theological research and engagement with democratic societies. Its leverage lies in its schools, universities and media and in its presence on every continent.

3.name: Pontificia Commissio Iustitia et Pax
3.english: Pontifical Commission for Justice and Peace
3.text:
The Pontifical Commission for Justice and Peace was established by Paul VI on 6 January 1967 to carry the Council's social teaching into the world, and his encyclical Populorum Progressio, published that March, became its charter. It is presided over by Cardinal Maurice Roy, Archbishop of Quebec, with the American Monsignor Joseph Gremillion as secretary, and works with lay economists, development experts and the World Council of Churches.

The Commission argues that development is the new name for peace: rich nations must transfer resources, fair trade must replace exploitation, and land reform and social welfare must reach the poor of Latin America, Africa and Asia. It is reformist and anti-revolutionary, Western in its institutions but critical of capitalism's excesses. Its leverage lies in papal backing and international prestige.
3.wiki: Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace

4.name: I Cattocomunisti
4.text:
The Catholic Communists are the heirs of the wartime Movement of Catholic Communists, a Roman group that fought in the Resistance and passed into the orbit of the Italian Communist Party after 1945. Their guiding mind is Franco Rodano, a devout Catholic intellectual who with the economist Claudio Napoleoni edits the Rivista Trimestrale and quietly advises the Communist leadership around Luigi Longo and Enrico Berlinguer.

They argue that Christians and communists can build a just society together, that the Church should accept the Communist Party as a legitimate force and lift the excommunication decreed in 1949, and that the Vatican's bond with the Christian Democrats should end. Small in number, they draw strength from dialogue circles, Christian workers in the Communist-led unions and the openness of the Council.

5.name: Comunità dell'Isolotto
5.text:
The Isolotto Community is the parish of a working-class quarter of Florence whose priest, Don Enzo Mazzi, was removed by Cardinal Ermenegildo Florit in December 1968 after defending students who had occupied Parma Cathedral. The parishioners refused to accept the decision and now celebrate mass every Sunday in the open square, a symbol for the base communities and dissenting priests multiplying across Italy.

The community rejects the authority of bishops imposed from above, the alliance between the Church and Christian Democratic power and the wealth of the institution. It calls for a poor Church run by its assemblies, solidarity with workers' struggles and the Third World, and dialogue with Marxists. Its leverage lies in the media attention it commands and in the restless Catholic youth of 1968.

6.name: Stowarzyszenie PAX
6.text:
The PAX Association was built after 1945 by Bolesław Piasecki, leader of the pre-war fascist National Radical Camp Falanga, who after his arrest by the Soviets in 1944 offered his services to the new communist order. Licensed by the regime, PAX runs publishing houses, newspapers and profitable enterprises, holds seats in the Sejm and offers Polish Catholics a church loyal to the People's Republic and its Soviet alliance.

PAX combines authoritarian nationalism and Catholic piety with acceptance of socialism, and it joined the regime's anti-Zionist campaign of 1968. Rome put its weekly on the Index in 1955 and Cardinal Wyszyński's bishops shun it, yet PAX courts the Curia as an alternative channel to Warsaw. Its leverage lies in state money, the security services and Piasecki's ambition.

7.name: Opus Pacis
7.text:
Opus Pacis is the Catholic committee of Hungary's National Peace Council, set up in 1957 after the crushing of the revolution to bind the clergy to the communist state. Steered by the State Office for Church Affairs, it gathers the so-called peace priests, who hold key posts in dioceses and chanceries, while Cardinal József Mindszenty remains a refugee in the American embassy in Budapest.

Its leaders preach loyalty to the People's Republic and to the Soviet peace policy, denounce the Vatican's old anti-communism and often report on fellow priests to the state. They see Casaroli's diplomacy since the partial agreement of 1964 as their opening to Rome. Their leverage lies in the state's control of appointments, salaries and seminaries, backed by the security police, over a frightened and divided clergy.

8.name: al-Majlis al-Islami al-Shi'i al-A'la
8.text:
The Supreme Islamic Shia Council was created by Lebanese law in 1967 to give the country's Shia community its own institutions, and in 1969 Imam Musa al-Sadr, an Iranian-born cleric settled in Tyre, became its first chairman. Sadr cultivates warm relations with Lebanon's Maronite and Greek Catholic bishops and is a natural interlocutor for the apostolic nunciature in Beirut.

The Council seeks justice for the neglected Shia of the south and the Bekaa within Lebanon's confessional system, pressing for schools, roads and representation rather than revolution. Sadr preaches the coexistence of the faiths and resistance to Israeli raids. For the Holy See he is an indispensable partner in preserving the Christian-Muslim balance of Lebanon, the only Arab state with a Christian president.

9.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
9.text:
The Islamic Dawa Party is a clandestine Iraqi Shia movement formed in Najaf in the late 1950s by young clerics and laymen around Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. Since the Ba'athist regime turned on the Najaf seminaries in 1969, expelling foreign students and arresting clerics, its members face arrest and torture, while Iraq's Chaldean and Syriac Catholics watch the same regime with growing unease.

Dawa calls for an Islamic state guided by the Shia jurists, rejecting both Western liberalism and Ba'athist socialism, and builds a disciplined network of cells among students, merchants and professionals. It has no dealings with the Holy See, but its rise matters to Rome: an Islamic order in Iraq would reshape the life of one of the oldest Christian communities of the East.

10.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
10.text:
The Muslim World League was founded in Mecca in 1962 on the initiative of Saudi Arabia's Prince Faisal, king since 1964, to spread Islam, fund mosques and rally the Muslim world against secular nationalism and communism. After the arson at Jerusalem's al-Aqsa Mosque in August 1969, Faisal's diplomacy brought Muslim heads of state to the Rabat summit of September, which resolved to create a permanent Islamic Conference.

The League promotes the conservative Wahhabi reading of Islam backed by Saudi oil wealth, staunchly anti-communist and aligned in practice with the West. For the Holy See it is both partner and rival: it shares Rome's hostility to atheist communism and its anxiety over Israeli control of Jerusalem's holy places, but competes for converts in Africa and Asia.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and is banned across the Arab world for its attempts to win over army officers. Since Israel's occupation of East Jerusalem in 1967 its members in the Old City and the West Bank work underground, a few streets from the Christian holy places whose fate preoccupies the Holy See.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim regime, demanding a restored caliphate that would unite the Islamic world against both Western and Soviet power and rule Jerusalem under Islamic law, with Christians as protected minorities. It renounces armed action for now. Its leverage lies in disciplined cells, study circles and a patient strategy of winning officers to its cause.

12.name: Centre Islamique de Genève
12.text:
The Islamic Centre of Geneva was founded in 1961 by Said Ramadan, son-in-law of Hassan al-Banna and the Muslim Brotherhood's leading exile in Europe, after Nasser's persecution drove him from Egypt. From Geneva he publishes the review Al-Muslimun, receives Brotherhood exiles from Egypt and Syria and keeps contact with Muslim student associations across Western Europe, including Italy.

The Centre presents Islam as a complete system of faith, law and social order and seeks to Islamise societies gradually through preaching and education, rejecting Arab socialism and communism alike. It addresses Christians in the language of shared faith against materialism. For the Holy See it is the most articulate voice of political Islam in Europe, a partner against atheism but a rival in the Third World.

13.name: Secretaria Status
13.text:
The Secretariat of State has become the nerve centre of the Church since Paul VI's reform of the Roman Curia in 1967 placed it above the old congregations. It is headed since May 1969 by the French Cardinal Jean Villot, but its real engine is the Substitute, Archbishop Giovanni Benelli, while Archbishop Agostino Casaroli conducts relations with states as secretary of the Council for the Public Affairs of the Church.

Under Paul VI's guidance the Secretariat pursues a diplomacy above the blocs: appeals for peace in Vietnam, support for the United Nations, development aid and patient negotiation with the communist governments of Eastern Europe to save the Church's hierarchy. Its leverage lies in control of appointments, papal correspondence and the nunciatures, its eyes and ears in every capital.

14.name: Coetus Internationalis Patrum
14.text:
The International Group of Fathers was the traditionalist caucus of the Second Vatican Council, led by Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, Bishop Antônio de Castro Mayer of Campos and Archbishop Geraldo de Proença Sigaud of Diamantina. Its network survives: in September 1969 its circle helped prepare the critical study of the new Order of Mass presented to Paul VI by Cardinals Ottaviani and Bacci, and in October Lefebvre began training seminarians at Fribourg.

They defend the Latin Mass, the condemnation of liberalism and religious liberty, and the authority of tradition against what they see as Protestant and modernist infiltration. Indifferent to Cold War diplomacy, they want a Church that converts rather than dialogues. Their leverage lies in the faithful alienated by liturgical reform and lay groups such as Una Voce.

14.name: Fraternitas Sacerdotalis Sancti Pii X
14.text:
The Society of Saint Pius X was canonically erected on 1 November 1970 by Bishop François Charrière of Lausanne, Geneva and Fribourg as a priestly fraternity under Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, who has opened a seminary at Écône in the Swiss Valais. It gathers young men from France, Switzerland, Germany and America who wish to be formed for the priesthood in the traditional manner.

The Society defends the Latin Mass and the pre-conciliar catechism, rejects religious liberty, ecumenism and collegiality, and regards the reforms of Paul VI as a betrayal of tradition. Indifferent to the Cold War blocs, it seeks a Church that converts rather than dialogues. Its leverage lies in traditionalist laity and in sympathetic bishops such as Antônio de Castro Mayer of Campos.

15.name: Istituto per le Opere di Religione
15.english: Institute for the Works of Religion
15.native_full: Istituto per le Opere di Religione
15.text:
The Institute for the Works of Religion, founded in 1942, is the Vatican's bank, managing the funds of religious orders, dioceses and Catholic institutions worldwide. Alongside the Administration of the Patrimony of the Holy See it controls large holdings in Italian banks, utilities and property. Bishop Paul Marcinkus of Chicago, consecrated by Paul VI in January 1969, is its secretary and rising power, and the Sicilian financier Michele Sindona its trusted partner.

After Italy ended the tax exemption on Vatican share dividends, the Institute began moving capital abroad through Sindona, who in 1969 acquired the Holy See's controlling stake in the Società Generale Immobiliare. Discreet and largely unaccountable, this financial circle values secrecy, profit and Western capital markets. Its leverage lies in the money that keeps the Holy See afloat.
15.wiki: Institute for the Works of Religion

16.name: Unione Cristiana Imprenditori Dirigenti
16.text:
The Christian Union of Business Executives was founded in Italy in 1947 to gather Catholic entrepreneurs and managers who wished to run their firms according to the Church's social teaching. A member of UNIAPAC, the international union of Christian employers, it counts industrialists, bankers and managers from Milan, Turin and Genoa, and keeps close ties with the Roman Curia and the Christian Democrats.

UCID defends private property, free enterprise and the market economy as the natural order of a Christian society, rejecting Marxist collectivism and distrusting the expanding state holdings favoured by Italy's centre-left. It favours a reading of Populorum Progressio that reforms capitalism rather than condemns it. Its leverage lies in the money, expertise and patronage its members lend to Catholic institutions.

17.name: Ordo Fratrum Minorum
17.text:
The Order of Friars Minor, the largest branch of the Franciscan family with some 25,000 friars, guards the memory of Saint Francis of Assisi, whose Canticle of the Creatures praises Brother Sun and Sister Water. In 1967 the American historian Lynn White proposed Francis as the patron saint of ecologists, and friars from Assisi to the missions are beginning to speak of creation as a trust endangered by industry.

They call for a simpler, poorer Church, respect for animals, forests and water as fellow creatures, and restraint in the exploitation of the earth that technology makes possible. They stand apart from the blocs and their arms race. Their leverage lies in the moral authority of the Poverello, their worldwide network of houses and the Custody of the Holy Land.

18.name: Movimiento de Sacerdotes para el Tercer Mundo
18.english: Movement of Priests for the Third World
18.native_full: Movimiento de Sacerdotes para el Tercer Mundo
18.text:
The Movement of Priests for the Third World was founded in Argentina in 1967 and 1968 by priests who answered the manifesto of eighteen Third World bishops inspired by Dom Hélder Câmara of Recife. Under its general secretary Miguel Ramondetti and figures such as Carlos Mugica, chaplain to the slums of Buenos Aires, it unites several hundred priests in open conflict with General Onganía's dictatorship and with many bishops.

The movement reads the gospel through the Medellín conference of 1968: the poor must be freed from dependence on foreign capital and local oligarchies, and many members see a Latin American socialism, even Peronism, as the road. Neither Atlanticist nor Soviet, it seeks a Church of the poor. Its leverage lies in the slums and the prestige of Third World bishops.
18.wiki: Movement of Priests for the Third World

19.name: Grupo Golconda
19.text:
The Golconda Group is a circle of some fifty Colombian priests who first met in July 1968 at the Golconda estate near Viotá and in December 1968 issued a declaration calling for socialism. Its patron is Gerardo Valencia Cano, Bishop of Buenaventura, and its inspiration is Camilo Torres, the priest and sociologist killed in 1966 fighting with the National Liberation Army.

The group holds that the Church must take sides in the class struggle, denounces the oligarchic order of the National Front and American imperialism, and looks to a Colombian socialism independent of Moscow, inspired by Cuba and by Marxist analysis. Some members sympathise openly with the guerrillas. Its leverage lies in a radicalised clergy, student and peasant movements, and the example it sets for priests across Latin America.

20.name: Sociedade Brasileira de Defesa da Tradição, Família e Propriedade
20.native_full: Sociedade Brasileira de Defesa da Tradição, Família e Propriedade
20.text:
The Brazilian Society for the Defence of Tradition, Family and Property was founded in São Paulo in 1960 by the Catholic writer Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira, author of Revolution and Counter-Revolution. With its red standards, golden lions and street campaigns of young militants it has spread to Argentina, Chile and Uruguay, and in 1968 it sent Paul VI a petition with well over a million signatures against leftist infiltration of the Church.

The TFP wages a crusade against land reform, socialism and progressive clergy, praises Brazil's military rulers as defenders of Christian civilisation and denounces Dom Hélder Câmara as a red archbishop. It wants a hierarchical Catholic society defended by the West. Its leverage lies in mass mobilisation, landowners' money and fervent youth.

21.name: Fuerza Nueva
21.text:
Fuerza Nueva is the publishing house and review founded in Madrid in 1966 by the notary Blas Piñar, a former director of the Institute of Hispanic Culture and a member of Franco's Cortes. It rallies Falangist veterans, Carlist hardliners and Catholic integrists who believe that Francoism is drifting toward liberalism under the technocrats and that the Church is betraying the crusade of 1936.

Fuerza Nueva demands a confessional, corporative state, the preservation of the 1953 Concordat with Franco's right to present bishops, and the silencing of the progressive clergy who shelter Basque nationalists and the Workers' Commissions. It denounces the Vatican's reforms and Paul VI's pressure on Spain's bishops. Its leverage lies in Civil War veterans, the diehards of the Movement and friends in the army.

22.name: Pontificia Cohors Helvetica
22.text:
The Pontifical Swiss Guard, raised in 1506 by Pope Julius II, is the oldest papal corps: about a hundred Catholic Swiss soldiers under Colonel Robert Nünlist who guard the Pope, the Apostolic Palace and the gates of the Vatican. Beside them serve the aristocratic Noble Guard, the volunteer Palatine Guard and the Pontifical Gendarmerie, relics of the Papal States in an age of reform.

The guards are sworn to give their lives for the Pope, and their loyalty is personal and absolute. They have no political programme, yet in a crisis of the papacy, a disputed succession or an attack on the Vatican they would be the only armed force able to secure the palace. Their leverage lies in their oath, their arms and five centuries of service.

23.name: Sancta Sedes
23.text:
The Holy See is the sovereign government of the Catholic Church and of the Vatican City State, an elective absolute monarchy whose ruler, Pope Paul VI, was elected in June 1963. Giovanni Battista Montini, former Archbishop of Milan and long a diplomat of the Secretariat of State, concluded the Second Vatican Council in 1965 and now governs some 600 million Catholics with supreme legislative, executive and judicial power.

Paul VI steers between reform and tradition: he has internationalised the Curia, promulgated the new Mass and travelled to the UN, India, Colombia and Uganda, yet he upheld clerical celibacy and condemned contraception in Humanae Vitae in 1968. He seeks peace between the blocs, dialogue with communist states and justice for the poor. His leverage is the papacy's spiritual authority.
